Oct 13 : Daily Mirror publisher Reach said on Tuesday digital revenue remained under pressure in the third quarter, and that it remained cautious about the segment's full-year outlook as industry-wide disruption weighed on audience traffic from Google. • News publishers are navigating falling print readership and weaker referral traffic from platforms such as Google amid the rise of AI chatbots. • Google's AI Overviews, which answer queries directly in search results, have drawn complaints from publishers over falling traffic and advertising revenue. • Reach's revenue fell 14.1 per cent in the quarter, with digital revenue down more than 20 per cent .

FAST

TAIPEI: The Trump administration opposes "coercion and aggression" by China against countries for exercising their sovereign rights, the US State Department said, after Beijing sanctioned Belizean and Paraguayan ministers over their ties to Taiwan. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said in response that the United States should "stop sending the wrong signals to Taiwan separatist forces". Paraguay and Belize are two of just 12 countries to maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. China says Taiwan is one of its provinces with no right to behave like a state, a view Taipei's government strongly rejects. The sanctions are largely symbolic because ministers from Taiwan's diplomatic allies generally do not travel to China. Beijing has previously imposed similar measures mainly on Western politicians for their support of democratically governed Taiwan.

"The Trump administration opposes coercion and aggression by China against countries in our hemisphere for exercising their sovereign rights," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement. Pigott cited previous comments by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the US "will not allow our region to become a base of operation for adversaries, competitors, and rivals to threaten our security or undermine our partnerships". "We stand with our friends and partners, including Taiwan, to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values," Pigott added. The United States is Taiwan's most important international backer, despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Washington has been concerned not only by Beijing's efforts to win over Taiwan's remaining allies, but also by attempts to increase its influence in Latin America.

TAIWAN'S VISIBILITY "GROWING HIGHER" Speaking on Tuesday (Oct 13) to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi said China was extending "transnational repression" to Taiwan's allies. "Taiwan's international visibility is growing higher and higher, and they will be kept busy by this fact," Chen said, referring to China. "Do they plan to sanction the whole world?" Taiwan Premier Cho Jung-tai said Beijing had no right to interfere in the domestic affairs of, or influence the diplomacy of, any sovereign and independent state, "including the Republic of China", referring to the island's formal name. "At the same time, we will resist any expansion of hegemony or authoritarianism," he added, also speaking at parliament. China has stepped up pressure on Taiwan's remaining diplomatic allies to sever ties with Taipei. The last country to do so was the tiny Pacific Island nation of Nauru, in 2024. Honduras ended its decades-long ties with Taiwan in 2023.

Source: Reuters/ec

FAST

MELBOURNE, Oct 13 : Wallabies back Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has endorsed his move to the wing, saying it will make him a better all-round player, as Australia continues to debate where the former rugby league sensation is best deployed. Suaalii has played predominantly in the centres since crossing from the National Rugby League's Sydney Roosters two years ago but Wallabies coach Les Kiss started him on the wing in the last two tests, including Saturday's 50-19 Bledisloe Cup thrashing by New Zealand at Eden Park. His ideal position continues to be a talking point in Australian rugby but the 23-year-old says his shift out wide can only accelerate his development. "Part of my journey of learning to be a great rugby player is to learn different positions, and I'm enjoying it," he told reporters on Tuesday.

"Seeing the game from a different perspective helps me be a better centre, helps me be a better fullback ... so I'm really enjoying it." Eden Park was a setback both for the Wallabies, who suffered their first test loss under Kiss, and for Suaalii, whose skills under the high ball were nullified by an All Blacks team who won the aerial battle decisively. The result also ended Australia's hopes of wresting back the Bledisloe Cup, with New Zealand retaining the annual trophy contested by the nations for a 24th straight year. Suaalii may yet end up redeployed in the midfield for the second Bledisloe test in Sydney on Saturday following injuries to Len Ikitau and Jordan Petaia, and Hunter Paisami's suspension.  He was confident the Wallabies would respond after Eden Park where they challenged for a half before being blown away. "We reviewed the game brutally and honestly as well," he said. “There’s a bigger plan to what we’re doing ... we’re real confident that this week we’ll be great.”

FAST

Oct 13 : Iga Swiatek has played at every edition of the WTA Finals since 2021, but with the Pole running out of time to claim a place at this year's season-ending tournament she knows the importance of going deep at her few remaining events. The six-time major champion has won only one tournament this year at the Canadian Open in August and failed to advance beyond the quarter-final stage at all four Grand Slams. The 25-year-old, who won the WTA Finals in 2023, is 10th in the qualifying table for the November 8-15 tournament at Indian Wells with only four of the eight spots still up for grabs. She sits on 3,799 points, 111 behind Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk in 9th place. Karolina Muchova, on 4,615 points, is the lowest-ranked player not to have sealed qualification.

"Obviously I'm aware of the situation and it would be great to get into the Finals, for sure it's our goal," Swiatek told reporters on Monday ahead of the Wuhan Open. "It's the first time I've faced a situation like that, to get into the finals. "It's a challenge, but I feel like it's a positive one and I'm really motivated ... There are still a few tournaments ahead." Swiatek said she had made some positive changes to her game under coach Francisco Roig, whom she appointed in April after parting ways with Wim Fissette. "I needed to change some stuff, and Francisco has a really great idea for my game, and I feel like we're developing my game on the practice court quite a lot, and it's been good progress," she added. "The US Open swing, for sure, was the most positive part of the season, so that shows that I'm going in the right direction." Swiatek, who faces compatriot Magdalena Frech in her opening match in Wuhan on Wednesday, is also scheduled to compete at WTA 500 events in Ningbo and Tokyo before the WTA Finals slots are wrapped up.

FAST

SYDNEY, Oct 13 : Code-hopping winger Mark Nawaqanitawase will not play for Australia in the Nations Championship in November and might consider representing Fiji or Italy at next year's Rugby World Cup, his agent told News Corp on Tuesday. Nawaqanitawase played 11 tests for the Wallabies and took part in the Paris Olympics for the Australia Sevens team before switching to rugby league with the Sydney Roosters in 2024.  He was always committed to returning to rugby union despite enjoying huge success in the 13-man code, representing Australia and New South Wales before finishing up by winning the National Rugby League (NRL) title with the Roosters earlier this month. The 26-year-old is contracted to Japan's Wild Knights for two years and will become eligible to play for Fiji and Italy next season through paternal and maternal heritage respectively.

With his heritage making him eligible to represent both Italy and Fiji, he remains open to all options regarding his international future. "At this stage, Mark’s priority is establishing himself in Japan and continuing to develop his rugby, with any future international decisions to be considered at the appropriate time." Australia will play England, Scotland and Wales in the Nations Championship in November and host the World Cup next year.

Oct 13 : Anthropic said on Monday its experiments suggested small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, such as smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.   • In its experiments, Anthropic looked at whether AI models could find vulnerable devices, copy themselves into those devices, and continue spreading without human help. • It found that small models under 30 billion parameters could complete the many steps needed for replication. • However, the firm found that such AI models also struggled to complete the entire sequence from start to finish.

• In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication. • Replicating models would be hard to shut down as there is no central switch-off point and, unlike non-AI malware, they could also figure out unfamiliar devices on their own, targeting data center processors, Anthropic warned. • The firm focused on IoT devices like Android TVs, smart appliances, and other internet-connected gadgets in its research as these are typically poorly secured. • The AI major also warned that if small models improved at their historical rate, they would be able to autonomously replicate by the end of this year, with small weight-based replicators following suit soon after. • Anthropic also said such autonomous AI systems were likely to replicate slowly and rely on widely available, relatively insecure computing resources. It added that systems should be strengthened to make it harder for such AI agents to spread.

Source: Reuters

Oct 13 : Czech arms maker CSG said on Tuesday it had acquired a 9.5 per cent stake in Canada's MDA Space, becoming the satellite and space technology company's largest shareholder. CSG said the investment was its first venture into the space sector and could lead to further cooperation, including joint investments in European manufacturing facilities and potential acquisitions. The company said it expects the global space economy to nearly triple to about $1.8 trillion by 2035.

Source: Reuters
